# Engage: Hurricane Sandy & the Moon

::: {.engage-box}
## 🌊 The Phenomenon: October 29, 2012

- **Date:** October 29, 2012 — Hurricane Sandy makes landfall during a **New Moon spring tide**
- **Surge Height:** ~14 ft storm surge at Battery Park, Manhattan — a historic record
- **Timing:** The New Moon brought the month's **highest spring tides** on the exact same night

### 🤔 Driving Questions:
- How do the **relative positions** of the Moon, Earth, and Sun create predictable tidal cycles?
- What is the connection between **moon phases** and ocean **tides**?
- How can **spring tides** make storm surges catastrophically more dangerous?
:::

## 🌙 Interactive: Explore Moon Phases

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {chart} from "@mbostock/phases-of-the-moon"

viewof year = Inputs.number({label: "Year", value: 2012, step: 1, min: 1900, max: 2100})

chart
```

::: {.student-task}
### 📝 Calendar Observations — Use the Interactive Above

1. Navigate to **October 2012**. What moon phase was occurring on **October 29** (Sandy's landfall)?
2. Count the days between two consecutive **New Moons**. What is the length of one lunar cycle?
3. Based on the pattern, how often does a **spring tide** (New or Full Moon) occur each month?
4. **Predict:** If Sandy had arrived on October 16 instead, what moon phase would it have been? Would tides be higher or lower?
:::

# Explore 1: The Lunar Cycle

::: {.explore-box}
## 🔬 Moon Illumination Through One Lunar Cycle

Study the chart below — it shows how much of the Moon's face is illuminated as seen from Earth across ~29.5 days.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot = require("@observablehq/plot")
d3 = require("d3@7")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
moonPhases = [
  {day: 0, phase: "New Moon", illumination: 0, icon: "🌑"},
  {day: 3.7, phase: "Waxing Crescent", illumination: 12.5, icon: "🌒"},
  {day: 7.4, phase: "First Quarter", illumination: 50, icon: "🌓"},
  {day: 11.1, phase: "Waxing Gibbous", illumination: 87.5, icon: "🌔"},
  {day: 14.8, phase: "Full Moon", illumination: 100, icon: "🌕"},
  {day: 18.5, phase: "Waning Gibbous", illumination: 87.5, icon: "🌖"},
  {day: 22.1, phase: "Third Quarter", illumination: 50, icon: "🌗"},
  {day: 25.8, phase: "Waning Crescent", illumination: 12.5, icon: "🌘"},
  {day: 29.5, phase: "New Moon", illumination: 0, icon: "🌑"}
]

Plot.plot({
  title: "Moon Illumination Through One Lunar Cycle",
  subtitle: "The moon takes ~29.5 days to complete one full cycle of phases",
  width: 700,
  height: 360,
  x: {label: "Day of Lunar Cycle", domain: [0, 30]},
  y: {label: "Illumination (%)", domain: [0, 110]},
  marks: [
    Plot.areaY(moonPhases, {x: "day", y: "illumination", fill: "#c0c0c0", fillOpacity: 0.2, curve: "natural"}),
    Plot.lineY(moonPhases, {x: "day", y: "illumination", stroke: "#555", strokeWidth: 2.5, curve: "natural"}),
    Plot.dot(moonPhases, {x: "day", y: "illumination", r: 8, fill: d => d.illumination > 50 ? "#f1c40f" : "#555", stroke: "#333", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
    Plot.text(moonPhases, {x: "day", y: "illumination", text: "icon", dy: -22, fontSize: 20}),
    Plot.text(moonPhases.filter(d => d.day === 0 || d.day === 7.4 || d.day === 14.8 || d.day === 22.1),
      {x: "day", y: "illumination", text: "phase", dy: 25, fontSize: 10, fontWeight: 600})
  ]
})
```

::: {.student-task}
### 📝 Interpret the Illumination Chart

1. On which day does illumination reach **100%**? What phase is this?
2. On which day does illumination reach **0%**? What phase is this?
3. What two phases occur when illumination is exactly **50%**? How many days apart are they?
4. **Connect to Sandy:** New Moons happen at **0% illumination**. Based on the chart, how often does a New Moon occur? How does this determine when spring tides happen?
:::

# Explain 1: The Geometry of Moon Phases

::: {.explain-box}
## 💡 Top-Down View: Why Do Phases Change?

The diagram below shows the Sun–Earth–Moon system from above the Solar System. Study the 4 major positions.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const width = 620, height = 440;
  const svg = d3.create("svg")
    .attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${width} ${height}`)
    .attr("width", width)
    .attr("height", height)
    .style("background", "#0a0a2e")
    .style("border-radius", "16px");

  const cx = width / 2, cy = height / 2;
  const orbitR = 148;

  // Defs: arrowhead marker
  const defs = svg.append("defs");
  defs.append("marker")
    .attr("id", "arrowYellow")
    .attr("viewBox", "0 0 10 10")
    .attr("refX", 8).attr("refY", 5)
    .attr("markerWidth", 6).attr("markerHeight", 6)
    .attr("orient", "auto")
    .append("path").attr("d", "M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z").attr("fill", "#f1c40f");

  // Sun label (far left, representing distant Sun)
  svg.append("text")
    .attr("x", 38).attr("y", cy - 18)
    .text("☀️ SUN").attr("fill", "#f1c40f").attr("font-size", 15)
    .attr("font-weight", "bold").attr("text-anchor", "middle");
  svg.append("text")
    .attr("x", 38).attr("y", cy - 2)
    .text("(far left)").attr("fill", "#f1c40f88").attr("font-size", 10)
    .attr("text-anchor", "middle");

  // Sunlight direction arrows
  [-22, 0, 22].forEach(offset => {
    svg.append("line")
      .attr("x1", 68).attr("y1", cy + offset)
      .attr("x2", cx - orbitR - 28).attr("y2", cy + offset)
      .attr("stroke", "#f1c40f").attr("stroke-width", 1.4)
      .attr("opacity", 0.6)
      .attr("marker-end", "url(#arrowYellow)");
  });

  // Orbit ring
  svg.append("circle")
    .attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", cy).attr("r", orbitR)
    .attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#334").attr("stroke-width", 1.5)
    .attr("stroke-dasharray", "6,4");

  // Earth
  svg.append("circle")
    .attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", cy).attr("r", 22)
    .attr("fill", "#1a5fb4").attr("stroke", "#2ecc71").attr("stroke-width", 2.5);
  svg.append("text")
    .attr("x", cx).attr("y", cy + 8)
    .text("🌍").attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("font-size", 22);

  // 4 Phase positions (Sun is to the LEFT → New Moon at angle 180°)
  const phases = [
    {angle: 180, name: "🌑 New Moon",      desc: "Between Earth & Sun", fill: "#111"},
    {angle: 90,  name: "🌓 First Quarter", desc: "90° from Sun",        fill: "#888"},
    {angle: 0,   name: "🌕 Full Moon",     desc: "Opposite the Sun",    fill: "#f1c40f"},
    {angle: 270, name: "🌗 Third Quarter", desc: "270° from Sun",       fill: "#888"}
  ];

  phases.forEach(p => {
    const rad = p.angle * Math.PI / 180;
    const mx = cx + orbitR * Math.cos(rad);
    const my = cy + orbitR * Math.sin(rad);

    svg.append("circle")
      .attr("cx", mx).attr("cy", my).attr("r", 14)
      .attr("fill", p.fill).attr("stroke", "#bbb").attr("stroke-width", 1.5);

    const lx = cx + (orbitR + 46) * Math.cos(rad);
    const ly = cy + (orbitR + 46) * Math.sin(rad);

    svg.append("text")
      .attr("x", lx).attr("y", ly - 4)
      .text(p.name)
      .attr("fill", "#fff").attr("font-size", 13).attr("font-weight", "bold")
      .attr("text-anchor", "middle");
    svg.append("text")
      .attr("x", lx).attr("y", ly + 13)
      .text(p.desc)
      .attr("fill", "#99aacc").attr("font-size", 10).attr("text-anchor", "middle");
  });

  // Caption
  svg.append("text")
    .attr("x", cx).attr("y", height - 10)
    .text("Top-down view — NOT to scale. Arrows show incoming sunlight direction.")
    .attr("fill", "#445566").attr("font-size", 10).attr("text-anchor", "middle");

  return svg.node();
}
```

**Moon phases result from our changing viewing angle as the Moon orbits Earth — NOT from Earth's shadow.**

::: {.student-task}
### 📝 Interpret the Geometry Diagram

1. In the diagram, which position places the Moon **directly between** Earth and the Sun? What phase does this produce, and why does it appear dark from Earth?
2. Which position has Earth **between** the Moon and the Sun? What phase is this, and why is it fully lit?
3. **Write one sentence** explaining why the Full Moon always rises as the Sun sets.
4. **Misconception bust:** A classmate says "Moon phases are caused by Earth's shadow blocking the Moon." Use the diagram to explain why this is incorrect.
:::

# Explore 2: NYC Tide Heights — October 2012

::: {.explore-box}
## 🔬 Is There a Connection Between Moon Phase and Tide Height?

Study the graph below. It shows simulated tide heights for New York Harbor throughout October 2012. Vertical markers show the Full Moon, New Moon, and Sandy's landfall.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
tideData = {
  const data = [];
  for (let day = 1; day <= 31; day++) {
    for (let hour = 0; hour < 24; hour += 0.5) {
      const t = (day - 1) * 24 + hour;
      const semidiurnal = Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * t / 12.42);
      const springNeap = 1 + 0.35 * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * (day - 15) / 14.75);
      const height = semidiurnal * springNeap * 2.5 + 0.3;
      data.push({
        day: day + hour / 24,
        height: Math.round(height * 100) / 100,
        date: `Oct ${day}`
      });
    }
  }
  return data;
}

Plot.plot({
  title: "NYC Tide Heights — October 2012",
  subtitle: "Full Moon (Oct 15) · New Moon + Sandy's Landfall (Oct 29)",
  width: 720,
  height: 420,
  x: {label: "Day of October", domain: [1, 31]},
  y: {label: "Tide Height (feet)", domain: [-4, 5]},
  marks: [
    Plot.lineY(tideData, {x: "day", y: "height", stroke: "#2980b9", strokeWidth: 1.4}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#777", strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),

    // Full Moon — Oct 15
    Plot.ruleX([15], {stroke: "#f1c40f", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.text([{x: 15, y: 4.6}], {x: "x", y: "y",
      text: () => "🌕 Full Moon\nOct 15", fill: "#f1c40f",
      fontSize: 13, fontWeight: "bold", textAnchor: "middle"}),

    // New Moon — Oct 29
    Plot.ruleX([29], {stroke: "#d0d0d0", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.text([{x: 28.2, y: 4.6}], {x: "x", y: "y",
      text: () => "🌑 New Moon\nOct 29", fill: "#d0d0d0",
      fontSize: 13, fontWeight: "bold", textAnchor: "middle"}),

    // Sandy Landfall — Oct 29.8 (evening)
    Plot.ruleX([29.8], {stroke: "#e74c3c", strokeWidth: 3, strokeDasharray: "8,3"}),
    Plot.text([{x: 30, y: -2.8}], {x: "x", y: "y",
      text: () => "⚠️ SANDY\nLandfall", fill: "#e74c3c",
      fontSize: 13, fontWeight: "bold", textAnchor: "start"}),

    // Neap tide labels
    Plot.text([{x: 7.5, y: 4.4}], {x: "x", y: "y",
      text: () => "Neap Tide", fill: "#3498db", fontSize: 11, fontWeight: "bold", textAnchor: "middle"}),
    Plot.text([{x: 22, y: 4.4}], {x: "x", y: "y",
      text: () => "Neap Tide", fill: "#3498db", fontSize: 11, fontWeight: "bold", textAnchor: "middle"})
  ]
})
```

::: {.student-task}
### 📝 Tide Chart Analysis

1. On which days are the **tallest high tides** visible in the graph? Which annotated Moon phase marker are they closest to?
2. On which days are the **smallest tides** (neap tides) visible? What Moon phase creates neap tides?
3. Sandy's landfall (red dashed line) falls right next to which Moon phase marker? What does this tell you about why the flooding was so severe?
4. **Describe the pattern** in one sentence: How does Moon phase relate to tide height?
:::

# Explain 2: Spring vs. Neap Tides

::: {.explain-box}
## 💡 Gravitational Alignment Controls Tidal Range
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
tidalRange = [
  {phase: "New Moon\n(Spring Tide)", high: 3.4, low: -3.2, type: "spring", icon: "🌑"},
  {phase: "First Quarter\n(Neap Tide)", high: 2.0, low: -1.8, type: "neap", icon: "🌓"},
  {phase: "Full Moon\n(Spring Tide)", high: 3.4, low: -3.2, type: "spring", icon: "🌕"},
  {phase: "Third Quarter\n(Neap Tide)", high: 2.0, low: -1.8, type: "neap", icon: "🌗"}
]

Plot.plot({
  title: "Spring Tides vs. Neap Tides: Tidal Range by Moon Phase",
  subtitle: "Spring tides (Sun–Moon aligned) produce much larger tidal swings",
  width: 600,
  height: 380,
  x: {label: "Moon Phase", domain: tidalRange.map(d => d.phase)},
  y: {label: "Tide Height (feet)", domain: [-4, 4]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Spring Tide", "Neap Tide"], range: ["#e74c3c", "#3498db"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.barY(tidalRange, {x: "phase", y: "high", fill: d => d.type === "spring" ? "#e74c3c" : "#3498db", tip: true}),
    Plot.barY(tidalRange, {x: "phase", y: "low", fill: d => d.type === "spring" ? "#e74c3c" : "#3498db", fillOpacity: 0.5}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#333", strokeWidth: 1.5}),
    Plot.text(tidalRange, {x: "phase", y: d => d.high + 0.4, text: "icon", fontSize: 22})
  ]
})
```

- 🌑🌕 **Sun–Moon Aligned (New / Full Moon) → Gravitational forces ADD together → Spring Tide** (largest range)
- 🌓🌗 **Sun–Moon at 90° (Quarter Moons) → Gravitational forces CANCEL partially → Neap Tide** (smallest range)

::: {.student-task}
### 📝 Spring vs. Neap — Use the Bar Chart Above

1. By approximately how many feet does a spring tide **exceed** a neap tide (read from the bar chart)?
2. Sandy's surge added ~5 ft on top of the high tide. The Oct 29 spring tide was ~3.4 ft; a typical neap tide is ~2.0 ft. Calculate the approximate total flood height for each scenario. What is the difference?
3. **Draw a diagram** showing Sun–Earth–Moon positions for: **(a)** a spring tide, **(b)** a neap tide. Mark the tidal bulges and label gravitational forces.
:::

# Elaborate: Why Are Eclipses Rare?

::: {.elaborate-box}
## 🔭 Inquiry Task: The Moon's 5° Orbital Tilt

New Moons happen every ~29.5 days — so why isn't there a solar eclipse every New Moon?

**Study the diagram below. Use only what you can observe in it to answer the questions.**
:::

![Moon's 5° Orbital Tilt relative to the Ecliptic plane](images/moon-orbital-tilt.png){fig-alt="Side-view diagram showing the Moon's orbit tilted approximately 5 degrees above and below Earth's orbital plane (the ecliptic). The Moon passes above or below the Sun–Earth line most months, only crossing the ecliptic at two orbital nodes." width="640"}

::: {.student-task}
### 📝 Deduce from the Diagram

1. Based on the diagram, does the Moon's orbit always line up **directly** with the Sun–Earth line? What does the diagram show happening most of the time?
2. The two points where the Moon crosses Earth's orbital plane are called **nodes**. How rarely do these crossings line up with a New or Full Moon?
3. **Claim + Evidence:** Write a 2–3 sentence argument explaining why solar and lunar eclipses are rare. Cite only evidence visible in the diagram.
4. **Connect back:** Spring tides happen every ~2 weeks. Eclipses happen ~2–5 times per year. Which poses a **more frequent, predictable risk** for coastal storm flooding? Explain.
:::

::: {.mind-blown}
🌊 Hurricane Sandy arrived October 29, 2012 — New Moon spring tide. Gravitational forces aligned. Tides surged to their monthly peak. Sandy's storm surge was added on top. The result: a historic catastrophe.
:::

```{=html}
  <div id="mmf-feedback" style="margin-top:16px; padding:16px; border-radius:10px; display:none; font-size:0.95em; line-height:1.6;"></div>
  <button id="mmf-next" onclick="mmfNext()" style="display:none; margin-top:12px; width:100%; padding:12px; border:2px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.2); border-radius:10px; background:transparent; color:white; font-size:0.95em; font-weight:600; cursor:pointer;">Next Card →</button>
  <div id="mmf-done" style="display:none; text-align:center; padding:20px;">
    <div style="font-size:2.5em; margin-bottom:10px;">🎉</div>
    <div style="font-size:1.3em; font-weight:700;">All cards complete!</div>
    <div style="color:#94a3b8; margin:8px 0;">Final score: <span id="mmf-final" style="color:#74b9ff; font-weight:700;"></span> / 8</div>
    <button onclick="mmfRestart()" style="margin-top:12px; padding:10px 24px; border:2px solid #74b9ff; border-radius:20px; background:transparent; color:#74b9ff; font-size:0.9em; cursor:pointer; font-weight:600;">Play Again</button>
  </div>
</div>
<script>
(function() {
  var cards = [
    {
      text: "Moon phases are caused by Earth's shadow falling on the Moon.",
      type: "Myth",
      explanation: "Earth's shadow causes a lunar eclipse — a rare event. Moon phases happen every month and are caused by our changing viewing angle as the Moon orbits Earth. The illuminated half always faces the Sun; what changes is how much of it we can see."
    },
    {
      text: "\"Spring tides\" only happen in the spring season (March–May).",
      type: "Myth",
      explanation: "The term 'spring' comes from the Old English word springan meaning 'to leap' — not the season. Spring tides happen every ~2 weeks, at every New Moon and Full Moon, year-round, whenever the Sun and Moon are gravitationally aligned."
    },
    {
      text: "A Full Moon occurs when Earth is approximately between the Sun and Moon.",
      type: "Fact",
      explanation: "Correct! At Full Moon, Earth sits between the Sun and the Moon, so the Moon's entire sunlit face points directly toward us. This is why we see a fully illuminated disk — and why the Full Moon always rises around sunset."
    },
    {
      text: "The Moon produces its own light that brightens and dims each month.",
      type: "Myth",
      explanation: "The Moon produces no light of its own. It reflects about 12% of the sunlight that hits it (its albedo). The Moon's surface brightness stays constant — what changes is how much of the lit side is visible from Earth as it orbits."
    },
    {
      text: "The timing of Hurricane Sandy's landfall during a New Moon made its flooding significantly worse.",
      type: "Fact",
      explanation: "Sandy made landfall October 29, 2012 — a New Moon spring tide. The already-elevated baseline tide added roughly 1–2 extra feet to the storm surge. The Battery gauge recorded a record ~14 ft surge. During a neap tide instead, total flood heights would have been measurably lower."
    },
    {
      text: "Solar eclipses don't happen every New Moon primarily because the Moon is sometimes too far from Earth.",
      type: "Myth",
      explanation: "Distance variation (apogee/perigee) affects eclipse type (total vs. annular), but the PRIMARY reason eclipses are rare is the Moon's 5° orbital tilt. Most months the Moon passes above or below the Sun–Earth line; only when a New or Full Moon coincides with an orbital node does an eclipse occur (~2–5 times per year)."
    },
    {
      text: "During a First or Third Quarter Moon, exactly half of the Moon's surface is illuminated by the Sun.",
      type: "Fact",
      explanation: "At Quarter Moons, the Moon is 90° from the Sun as seen from Earth, so we see exactly half the illuminated face. They're called 'quarters' because the Moon has completed one-quarter (or three-quarters) of its full orbit — not because only a quarter is lit."
    },
    {
      text: "Neap tides are dangerous because the water level drops to extremely low levels.",
      type: "Myth",
      explanation: "Neap tides produce the smallest tidal range — moderate highs and moderate lows, not dangerous extremes. The real coastal hazard comes from spring tides (New and Full Moon), which produce the highest high tides. A spring-tide baseline dramatically amplifies storm surge flooding."
    }
  ];
  var idx = 0, score = 0, answered = 0, cardAnswered = false;
  function updateCard() {
    if (idx >= cards.length) {
      document.getElementById('mmf-card').style.display = 'none';
      document.getElementById('mmf-myth').style.display = 'none';
      document.getElementById('mmf-fact').style.display = 'none';
      document.getElementById('mmf-feedback').style.display = 'none';
      document.getElementById('mmf-next').style.display = 'none';
      document.getElementById('mmf-done').style.display = 'block';
      document.getElementById('mmf-final').textContent = score;
      return;
    }
    document.getElementById('mmf-card').textContent = cards[idx].text;
    document.getElementById('mmf-progress').textContent = 'Card ' + (idx + 1) + ' of ' + cards.length;
    document.getElementById('mmf-feedback').style.display = 'none';
    document.getElementById('mmf-next').style.display = 'none';
    document.getElementById('mmf-myth').disabled = false;
    document.getElementById('mmf-fact').disabled = false;
    document.getElementById('mmf-myth').style.opacity = '1';
    document.getElementById('mmf-fact').style.opacity = '1';
    cardAnswered = false;
  }
  window.mmfAnswer = function(choice) {
    if (cardAnswered) return;
    cardAnswered = true;
    answered++;
    var card = cards[idx];
    var correct = (choice === card.type);
    if (correct) score++;
    document.getElementById('mmf-score').textContent = score;
    document.getElementById('mmf-total').textContent = answered;
    var fb = document.getElementById('mmf-feedback');
    fb.style.display = 'block';
    fb.style.background = correct ? 'rgba(0,184,148,0.2)' : 'rgba(214,48,49,0.2)';
    fb.style.border = '1px solid ' + (correct ? '#00b894' : '#e17055');
    fb.innerHTML = '<strong>' + (correct ? '✅ Correct! ' : '❌ That\'s a ' + card.type + '! ') + '</strong>' + card.explanation;
    document.getElementById('mmf-myth').disabled = true;
    document.getElementById('mmf-fact').disabled = true;
    document.getElementById('mmf-myth').style.opacity = (choice === 'Myth') ? '1' : '0.5';
    document.getElementById('mmf-fact').style.opacity = (choice === 'Fact') ? '1' : '0.5';
    document.getElementById('mmf-next').style.display = 'block';
  };
  window.mmfNext = function() { idx++; updateCard(); };
  window.mmfRestart = function() {
    idx = 0; score = 0; answered = 0;
    document.getElementById('mmf-card').style.display = 'flex';
    document.getElementById('mmf-myth').style.display = 'block';
    document.getElementById('mmf-fact').style.display = 'block';
    document.getElementById('mmf-done').style.display = 'none';
    document.getElementById('mmf-score').textContent = '0';
    document.getElementById('mmf-total').textContent = '0';
    updateCard();
  };
  updateCard();
})();
</script>
```

## 🧠 Comprehensive Unit Quiz

Test your complete understanding of moon phases, tides, and storm science!

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
function buildUnitQuiz(id, title, questions) {
  const outer = html`<div id="${id}" style="font-family:'Inter',sans-serif; max-width:720px; margin:18px auto;"></div>`;
  const header = html`<div style="background:linear-gradient(135deg,#667eea 0%,#764ba2 100%);color:#fff;border-radius:14px 14px 0 0;padding:18px 24px;">
    <div style="font-size:1.1em;font-weight:700;display:flex;align-items:center;gap:8px;"><span style="font-size:1.2em;">📝</span> ${title}</div>
    <div style="font-size:0.85em;opacity:0.85;margin-top:4px;">Select an answer for each question.</div>
  </div>`;
  const body = html`<div style="border:1.5px solid #c7d2fe;border-top:none;border-radius:0 0 14px 14px;overflow:hidden;background:#f8f9ff;padding:16px;"></div>`;
  questions.forEach((qq, qi) => {
    const card = document.createElement("div");
    card.style.cssText = "background:#fff;border-radius:12px;padding:16px 20px;margin-bottom:14px;box-shadow:0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.08);";
    card.innerHTML = `<p style="font-weight:700;margin:0 0 10px;color:#1e1b4b;">${qi+1}. ${qq.q}</p>`;
    qq.options.forEach((opt, oi) => {
      const btn = document.createElement("button");
      btn.textContent = opt;
      btn.style.cssText = "display:block;width:100%;text-align:left;padding:10px 14px;margin:6px 0;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;cursor:pointer;font-size:.95em;transition:border-color .2s,background .2s;";
      btn.onmouseover = () => { if(!card.dataset.answered){ btn.style.borderColor="#667eea";btn.style.background="#f0f0ff"; }};
      btn.onmouseout  = () => { if(!card.dataset.answered){ btn.style.borderColor="#e2e8f0";btn.style.background="#fff"; }};
      btn.onclick = () => {
        if(card.dataset.answered) return;
        card.dataset.answered = "true";
        card.querySelectorAll("button").forEach(b => {
          b.style.cursor="default"; b.onmouseover=null; b.onmouseout=null;
          b.style.borderColor="#e2e8f0"; b.style.background="#f8fafc"; b.style.color="#475569";
        });
        if(oi === qq.correct){
          btn.style.borderColor="#48bb78";btn.style.background="#f0fff4";btn.style.color="#276749";btn.style.fontWeight="700";
          fb.innerHTML = "✅ Correct! " + qq.explanation;
          fb.style.color="#276749";fb.style.background="#f0fff4";
        } else {
          btn.style.borderColor="#fc8181";btn.style.background="#fff5f5";btn.style.color="#9b2c2c";btn.style.fontWeight="700";
          const correctBtn = card.querySelectorAll("button")[qq.correct];
          correctBtn.style.borderColor="#48bb78";correctBtn.style.background="#f0fff4";correctBtn.style.color="#276749";correctBtn.style.fontWeight="700";
          fb.innerHTML = "❌ " + qq.explanation;
          fb.style.color="#9b2c2c";fb.style.background="#fff5f5";
        }
        fb.style.padding="10px 14px";fb.style.marginTop="8px";fb.style.borderRadius="8px";
      };
      card.appendChild(btn);
    });
    const fb = document.createElement("div");
    fb.style.cssText = "border-radius:8px;font-size:.9em;transition:all .3s;";
    card.appendChild(fb);
    body.appendChild(card);
  });
  outer.appendChild(header);
  outer.appendChild(body);
  return outer;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
buildUnitQuiz("moon-unit-quiz", "🧠 Comprehensive Unit Quiz — Moon Phases, Tides & Storms", [
  {
    q: "What is the PRIMARY cause of moon phases?",
    options: [
      "Earth's shadow falls on the Moon as it orbits",
      "The Moon moves closer to and farther from Earth each month",
      "Our viewing angle changes as the Moon orbits Earth, revealing different portions of its sunlit half",
      "Clouds and atmosphere filter how much of the Moon we can see"
    ],
    correct: 2,
    explanation: "Moon phases result entirely from geometry — as the Moon orbits, we see different fractions of its always-half-illuminated surface. Earth's shadow causes lunar eclipses, not phases."
  },
  {
    q: "How long does one complete lunar cycle (New Moon to New Moon) take?",
    options: ["~24 hours", "~7 days", "~29.5 days", "~365 days"],
    correct: 2,
    explanation: "The synodic lunar cycle takes approximately 29.5 days — this is why we see roughly one full set of phases each calendar month."
  },
  {
    q: "At which moon phase(s) do Spring Tides occur?",
    options: [
      "Only at Full Moon",
      "Only at New Moon",
      "At both New Moon and Full Moon",
      "At First Quarter and Third Quarter"
    ],
    correct: 2,
    explanation: "Spring tides happen when the Sun, Earth, and Moon are aligned — both at New Moon (Moon between Earth and Sun) and Full Moon (Earth between Moon and Sun). Gravitational forces combine in both configurations."
  },
  {
    q: "Hurricane Sandy made landfall on October 29, 2012. Which moon phase occurred that day, and how did it affect flooding?",
    options: [
      "Full Moon — the bright light helped people evacuate faster",
      "Third Quarter — neap tides reduced the storm surge impact",
      "New Moon — spring tide elevated the baseline water level, adding to the storm surge",
      "First Quarter — the tide was average, neither helping nor hurting"
    ],
    correct: 2,
    explanation: "Oct 29 was a New Moon, producing a spring tide. The already-elevated high tides added 1–2 ft to Sandy's surge, contributing to the record ~14 ft surge at Battery Park, Manhattan."
  },
  {
    q: "Why don't solar eclipses occur every New Moon?",
    options: [
      "The Moon is always on the wrong side of Earth during a New Moon",
      "The Moon's orbit is tilted ~5° relative to Earth's orbital plane, so it usually passes above or below exact alignment",
      "The Sun is too far away for the Moon's shadow to reach Earth",
      "Eclipses only happen at Full Moon, not New Moon"
    ],
    correct: 1,
    explanation: "The Moon's 5° orbital tilt means it usually passes slightly above or below the Sun–Earth line. Eclipses only occur when a New or Full Moon coincides with the Moon crossing Earth's orbital plane at an orbital node."
  },
  {
    q: "Which tidal pattern produces the SMALLEST difference between high tide and low tide?",
    options: [
      "Spring tides, occurring at New and Full Moon",
      "Neap tides, occurring at Quarter Moons",
      "King tides, occurring at solar equinoxes",
      "Tidal range is the same regardless of moon phase"
    ],
    correct: 1,
    explanation: "Neap tides occur when the Sun and Moon are at 90° to Earth. Their gravitational pulls partially cancel, producing moderate — not extreme — tidal ranges."
  },
  {
    q: "What does it mean for the Moon to have a 12% albedo?",
    options: [
      "The Moon produces 12% of the light that the Sun produces",
      "12% of the Moon's surface is visible from Earth at any time",
      "The Moon reflects 12% of the sunlight that hits its surface",
      "The Moon is 12% as large as Earth"
    ],
    correct: 2,
    explanation: "Albedo is the fraction of light a surface reflects. The Moon's rocky surface reflects only ~12% of incoming sunlight, making it far dimmer than the Sun — though bright enough to cast shadows on a dark night."
  },
  {
    q: "During a First Quarter Moon, where is the Moon relative to the Sun (as seen from Earth)?",
    options: [
      "Directly between Earth and the Sun (0°)",
      "On the opposite side of Earth from the Sun (180°)",
      "At 90° to the Sun",
      "At 45° to the Sun"
    ],
    correct: 2,
    explanation: "At First Quarter, the Moon is 90° from the Sun as seen from Earth — we see the right half illuminated. 'Quarter' refers to the Moon completing one-quarter of its orbit, not the fraction of the Moon lit."
  },
  {
    q: "How do rising sea levels caused by climate change interact with spring tide storm surges?",
    options: [
      "Rising sea levels cancel out spring tide effects, so future surges will be unchanged",
      "Rising sea levels raise the baseline water height, so the same spring tide + storm surge reaches higher total flood levels",
      "Climate change shortens the lunar cycle, creating more frequent spring tides",
      "Warmer water reduces the Moon's gravitational pull on the oceans"
    ],
    correct: 1,
    explanation: "Sea level rise doesn't change the tidal cycle — spring tides still happen every ~2 weeks. But a higher baseline means any given storm surge on top of a spring tide will reach higher total elevations, flooding areas that would previously have stayed dry."
  },
  {
    q: "If a powerful hurricane arrived during a Third Quarter neap tide instead of a New Moon spring tide, what would MOST LIKELY be true about the flooding?",
    options: [
      "Flooding would be more severe because Third Quarter tides are the highest",
      "Flooding would be about the same — moon phase doesn't affect storm surge",
      "Flooding would likely be less severe because neap tides have a lower baseline high-tide level",
      "Flooding would be less severe because neap tides pull water away from the coast"
    ],
    correct: 2,
    explanation: "Neap tides (Quarter Moons) produce lower-than-average high tides. If the storm arrived during a neap tide, the starting water level would be ~1.4 ft lower than a spring tide baseline — directly reducing the total combined flood height."
  }
])
```
